title: Universal edibility test for an unknown plant (last resort)
asks: how to test if a plant is edible
is this berry safe to eat
how do i know if a wild plant is poisonous
out of food can i eat plants i dont know
how long does the edibility test take
can i use the edibility test on mushrooms
how 2 tell if a plant is safe 2 eat
no food left, lots of plants around, how do we test them, over
answer: Use this test only as a last resort, when you cannot positively identify the plant. Positive identification is the best and safest method.

Test only one plant at a time, so that if something goes wrong it is obvious which plant caused it. Make sure there are enough of the plant to be worth the time and effort: each part of a plant takes more than 24 hours to test.
Smell the plant. If it has an unpleasant odor, such as a moldy or musty smell, or an almond scent, stop testing and disregard it as a possible food.
Crush or break part of the plant to see the color of its sap. If the sap is clear, proceed to the next step.
Touch the plant's sap or juice to your inner forearm. If there are no ill effects, such as a rash or a burning sensation, proceed.
Place some of the plant juice on your outer lip for 8 minutes. If a reaction occurs, stop the test.

If there is still no reaction, taste a small pinch of the plant and leave it in your mouth for 8 minutes. If there is an unpleasant taste, such as bitterness, or a numbing sensation of the tongue or lips, stop the test. If no reaction occurs, swallow the pinch.

After swallowing, wait 8 hours. If there is no reaction, chew a handful of the plant, swallow it, and wait an additional 8 hours. If no reaction occurs after those 8 hours, consider the tested plant part edible.
Eat any new or strange food with restraint until your body has become accustomed to it. The plant may be slightly toxic, and harmful when eaten in large quantities.
warnings: Do not use this test on mushrooms or fungi. The Army survival manual says to avoid them: there is no field test for determining whether an unknown mushroom or fungus is edible. The Forest Service mushroom guide in this library warns that mushroom consumption can pose a serious, even fatal, risk.
The same Army manual also says not to eat any plant unless you have positively identified it first. Ingestion poisoning can be very serious and could lead to death very quickly.

Berries: a berry you cannot positively identify is an unknown plant, and the test above is the last resort for it too. The Army survival manual says to avoid white and yellow berries, which are frequently poisonous, and that about half of all red berries are poisonous. The Army cold-weather manual describes baneberry, which it lists as poisonous: white or red berries with a black dot at the bottom opposite the stem, clustered on a central stalk, with white flesh. They are sometimes confused with cranberries, which are individual berries on several stalks, with red flesh and clear juice.

Stay away from wild or unknown plants that have: milky or discolored sap; beans, bulbs or seeds inside pods; a bitter or soapy taste; spines, fine hairs or thorns; foliage that resembles dill, carrot, parsnip or parsley; an almond scent in woody parts and leaves; grain heads with pink, purplish or black spurs; or a three-leafed growth pattern. Also consider plants with shiny leaves as poisonous, and avoid plants with umbrella-shaped flowers: water hemlock, one of the most poisonous plants, is a member of that family.

Water hemlock (Army cold-weather manual): one of the world's most poisonous plants. It can be recognized by where it grows, always in wet ground such as marshes and marshy lakes, and by a hollow, partitioned bulb at the base of a hollow stem, spindle-shaped roots, and a foul odor that is very noticeable in the root and bulb.

The Army manuals differ on how many plants are poisonous. The cold-weather manual says most plants that grow in cold regions can be eaten, and that water hemlock and baneberry are the only poisonous plants there. The survival manual lists other plants that cause poisoning if eaten (poison hemlock as well as water hemlock, and death camas among poisonous bulbs) and says not to eat any plant you have not positively identified. This card follows the survival manual: never treat an unknown plant as safe because it is not water hemlock or baneberry.

Signs of plant poisoning can include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, depressed heartbeat and breathing, headaches, hallucinations, dry mouth, unconsciousness and coma, which can lead to death.

If plant poisoning is suspected, the Army survival manual says to remove the poisonous material from the person's mouth and stomach as soon as possible. If the person is conscious: induce vomiting by tickling the back of the throat, and dilute the poison by giving large quantities of water or milk.

Limits on inducing vomiting, from the same library: only if the person is conscious. An Army medical manual, writing about radioactive material taken into the body, says agents that induce vomiting are contraindicated if the state of consciousness is impaired, such as in shock or drunkenness, or after swallowing corrosive agents or petroleum products. The Army survival manual says that if the poison is an acid, an alkali or a petroleum product (not a plant), vomiting should be avoided: the substance can burn the esophagus and can be inhaled into the lungs during vomiting.

Test all parts of the plant: some plants have both edible and inedible parts. Do not assume that a part that proved edible when cooked is also edible raw: test it raw before eating it raw. The same plant may produce varying reactions in different people.
It is risky to rely on a plant being edible because animals have been eating it: an animal may be able to digest toxins that a person cannot.
Eating large portions of plant food on an empty stomach may cause diarrhea, nausea or cramps. Even after testing a plant and finding it safe, eat it in moderation.
Heavy smokers are sometimes unable to taste various poisons. Keep a log of all plants eaten, and of plants identified as inedible when tested.

quotes.text: The best and safest method for edibility of a plant is positive identification of the plant. If positive identification is not possible, then use the edibility test.
There are exceptions to every rule, but isolated persons should only select unknown plants as a last resort.

Apply the edibility test to only one plant at a time so if some abnormality does occur, it will be obvious which plant caused the problem. Once a plant has been selected to be tested, proceed as follows:

Before testing a plant for edibility, make sure there are enough plants to make the testing worth the time and effort. Each part of a plant (roots, leaves, flowers, and so on) requires more than 24 hours to test. Do not waste time testing a plant that is not relatively abundant in the area.

Step 1. If there are any unpleasant odors such as a moldy or musty smell coming from the plant, stop testing and disregard as a possible edible plant option. Also, if the plant gives off an “almond” scent, disregard it as a possible edible plant option.
Step 2. Crush or break part of the plant to determine the color of its sap. If the sap is clear, proceed to the next step.
Step 3. Touch the plant's sap or juice to the inner forearm. If there are no ill effects, such as a rash or burning sensation to the skin, then proceed with the rest of the steps.
Step 4. If a there was not an ill reaction when touching the inner forearm, place some of the plant juice on the outer lip for eight minutes. If a reaction occurs, stop the test.

Step 5. If still no reaction, taste a small pinch of the plant and leave it in the mouth for eight minutes. If there is an unpleasant taste, such as bitterness or a numbing sensation of the tongue or lips, stop the test. If a reaction does not occur, swallow the pinch of plant.

Step 6. After swallowing, wait eight hours. If there is no reaction after eight hours, chew a handful of the plant, swallow, and wait an additional eight hours. If no reaction occurs after eight hours, consider the tested plant part edible.
Step 7. Eat any new or strange food with restraint until the body has become accustomed to it. The plant may be slightly toxic and harmful when eaten in large quantities.

Avoid mushrooms and fungi; they are not technically plants. Fungi have toxic peptides, a protein-based poison that has no taste. They are of little nutritional value and it is very difficult to determine if they are poisonous or safe to consume.

Mushroom consumption can pose a serious, even fatal, risk to humans. It is strongly recommended that you spend your first collecting season using field identifications guides and collecting with an expert if you intend to collect mushrooms to eat.
There is no field test for determining if an unknown mushroom or fungi is edible except by eating them. There are many poisonous varieties, and some wild mushrooms are hard for experts to identify.

Ingestion poisoning can be very serious and could lead to death very quickly. Isolated persons should not eat any plant unless they have positively identified it first. They should keep a log of all plants eaten and plants identified as inedible if tested.
Avoid white and yellow berries for they are frequently poisonous. About one-half of all red berries are poisonous.

Baneberries are normally found on hillsides or in forested bog areas. The white or red berries with a black dot at the bottom opposite the stem are clustered on a central stalk. (See figure 7-12.) The flesh is white. They are sometimes confused with cranberries, but cranberries are individual berries on several stalks. Cranberry flesh is red with clear juice.

Testing for edibility involves considerable time, so it is important to be proficient at identifying edible plants. To avoid potentially poisonous plants, stay away from any wild or unknown plants that have
Milky or discolored sap.
Beans, bulbs, or seeds inside pods.
A bitter or soapy taste.
Spines, fine hairs, or thorns.
Foliage that resembles dill, carrot, parsnip, or parsley.
An almond scent in woody parts and leaves.
Grain heads with pink, purplish, or black spurs.
A three-leafed growth pattern.
Consider plants with shiny leaves as poisonous.

Avoid plants with umbrella-shaped flowers although carrots, celery, dill, and parsley are members of this family (see figure 4-2 on page 4-9). One of the most poisonous plants, water hemlock, is also a member of this family.

Most plants that grow in cold regions can be eaten. The water hemlock and the baneberry are the only poisonous plants. Water hemlock is one of the world’s most poisonous plants and can be recognized by where it grows (always in wet ground) and by the following characteristics: a hollow, partitioned bulb at the base of a hollow stem, spindle-shaped roots, and a foul odor that is very noticeable in the root and bulb. The water hemlock is abundant in marshes near southern beaches and around marshy lakes in interior river valleys.
The following plants can cause ingestion poisoning if eaten:
Poison and water hemlocks.
Examples of poisonous bulbs include tulips and death camas.

Symptoms of ingestion poisoning can include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, depressed heartbeat and respiration, headaches, hallucinations, dry mouth, unconsciousness, coma; which can lead to death. If plant poisoning is suspected, try to remove the poisonous material from the victim's mouth and stomach as soon as possible. If the victim is conscious, induce vomiting by tickling the back of the victim's throat
If the victim is conscious, dilute the poison by administering large quantities of water or milk.

Emetics to induce vomiting. Emetics are most effective when taken with 200 to 300 milliliters of water. However, they are contraindicated if the state of consciousness is impaired, such as in the states of shock or inebriation or after ingestion of corrosive agents or petroleum hydrocarbons.

If the poison is an acid, an alkali, or a petroleum product, vomiting should be avoided because the substance can burn the esophagus. These types of products can also be inhaled into the lungs during vomiting

Test all parts of the plant for edibility, as some plants have both edible and inedible parts. Do not assume that a part that proved edible when cooked is also edible when raw. Test the part raw to ensure edibility before eating raw. The same part or plant may produce varying reactions in different individuals.
It is risky to rely on plants being edible for human consumption simply because animals have also been eating the plants. The animal may be able to digest certain toxins that a person cannot.

Remember that eating large portions of plant food on an empty stomach may cause diarrhea, nausea, or cramps. Two good examples of this are such familiar foods as green apples and wild onions. Even after testing plant food and finding it safe, eat it in moderation.
Sometimes heavy smokers are unable to taste various poisons, such as alkaloids.

conflict: (1) ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says in its survival-medicine chapter 'Isolated persons should not eat any plant unless they have positively identified it first', and in its food chapter gives this edibility test for unknown plants as a last resort; the card shows both. (2) Mushrooms: ATP 3-50.21 says 'Avoid mushrooms and fungi'; the kit also holds USDA Forest Service PNW-GTR-393 (wild edible mushrooms of the Blue Mountains), which describes edible species and cautions that 'Mushroom consumption can pose a serious, even fatal, risk'. Both agree that an unidentified mushroom must not be eaten; the card says not to use the test on mushrooms. (3) How many plants are poisonous (added in revision, shown in a warning): TC 21-3 (2025) para 7-40 says 'Most plants that grow in cold regions can be eaten. The water hemlock and the baneberry are the only poisonous plants', which is contradicted by ATP 3-50.21's list of plants that 'can cause ingestion poisoning if eaten' (castor bean, chinaberry, death camas, lantana, manchineel, oleander, pangi, physic nut, poison and water hemlocks, rosary pea, strychnine tree) and by its 'Examples of poisonous bulbs include tulips and death camas'. The card does not adopt TC 21-3's 'only' and says so; it does use TC 21-3's descriptions of water hemlock (7-40) and baneberry (7-41), leaving out 'It is never found on hillsides or dry ground'. (4) Inducing vomiting (owner decision open): ATP 3-50.21's first Ingestion Poisoning passage says 'If the victim is conscious, induce vomiting by tickling the back of the victim's throat or by giving the victim warm saltwater'; its second passage says vomiting should be avoided for an acid, an alkali or a petroleum product; ATP 4-02.83 (2014) para 4-27, written for clinicians treating internal radioactive contamination, says emetics are 'contraindicated if the state of consciousness is impaired, such as in the states of shock or inebriation or after ingestion of corrosive agents or petroleum hydrocarbons'. The revised card keeps 'conscious only', adds both limits, and leaves out the warm-saltwater method (the quote is cut just before it), on the reviewer's recommendation. The reviewer also flagged, from outside the kit, that current poison-control practice no longer advises inducing vomiting and that salt water given to cause vomiting can itself poison; no kit source says this, so the owner must decide whether to drop the induce-vomiting sentence altogether. (5) Berries (owner decision open): the card gives only the protective lines of ATP 3-50.21 para 4-50 ('Avoid white and yellow berries for they are frequently poisonous. About one-half of all red berries are poisonous.'). The same paragraph goes on 'Blue or black berries are generally safe for consumption' and 'Aggregated fruits and berries (for example, thimbleberry, raspberry, salmonberry, and blackberry) are always edible'; these generalizations are left off the card, as the reviewer left them to the owner. TC 21-3 para 7-42 adds only that cold regions 'have many kinds of berries that are edible'.

review.notes: Fail (one problem). (1) Previous findings fixed as asked: 'or by giving warm saltwater' is dropped (the quote is cut before it); ATP 3-50.21's second Ingestion Poisoning passage (avoid vomiting for an acid, alkali or petroleum product: it burns the esophagus and can be inhaled) and ATP 4-02.83 4-27 (emetics contraindicated when consciousness is impaired, in shock or inebriation, after corrosives or petroleum hydrocarbons; labelled as written about internal radioactive contamination) are added; the berry ask is answered with ATP 4-50's protective lines and TC 21-3 7-41's baneberry description, and the 'generally safe' and 'always edible' generalisations are left off; 'shiny leaves' added; TC 21-3 7-40's 'only poisonous plants' is shown attributed and not adopted; the water hemlock warning is added without TC's 'never on hillsides or dry ground' reassurance. Steps 1-9 re-checked against ATP 4-57/4-58, in order. (2) Remaining problem, vomiting: warning 8 still reads as an instruction to induce vomiting ('If the person is conscious: induce vomiting by tickling the back of the throat, and dilute the poison by giving large quantities of water or milk'). Only the sentence before it is attributed; its 'conscious' test is looser than the kit's own limit one line later (ATP 4-02.83: contraindicated if the state of consciousness is impaired), while the poisoning signs the card itself lists (hallucinations, depressed breathing, unconsciousness) are such impaired states; and the 'large quantities' of fluid have no limit at all. From outside the kit (flagged in the previous review, still unresolved): current first-aid and poison-control practice advises against inducing vomiting and against giving large volumes of fluid. Fix (recommended): drop the induce-vomiting and dilution sentence and the words 'and stomach'; keep 'remove the poisonous material from the person's mouth as soon as possible'; turn warning 9 into plain 'do not induce vomiting if...' lines (ATP 4-02.83: impaired consciousness, shock, drunkenness, corrosives, petroleum products; ATP 3-50.21: acid, alkali, petroleum product), and record ATP 3-50.21's recommendation in the conflict field. If the owner decides to keep the Army method, at minimum merge warnings 8 and 9 into one attributed line that leads with the contraindications, then 'the Army survival manual says...'. Minor: delete the editorial '(not a plant)' in warning 9; ATP does not say it. (3)-(6) Everything else passes: mushroom warnings (ATP, PNW-GTR-393), positive-identification conflict, avoid list, test every part and raw vs cooked, animals, empty stomach, smokers, log; conflicts attributed; kind protocol correct; all asks answered. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 xhigh) Fail. Steps 1-9 are faithful to ATP 3-50.21 4-57/4-58 in order (last resort, one plant at a time, abundance, more than 24 h per part, smell, sap, forearm, lip 8 min, mouth 8 min, swallow, 8 h, handful, 8 h, restraint); the mushroom warnings (ATP, PNW-GTR-393), the positive-ID conflict, avoid list, animals-eat-it risk, smokers, empty stomach and log are correct. Problems: (1) Drafter flag, inducing vomiting - verdict: faithful to ATP's first Ingestion Poisoning passage, but it omits the same chapter's limit in its second Ingestion Poisoning passage (the activated-charcoal paragraph): 'If the poison is an acid, an alkali, or a petroleum product, vomiting should be avoided because the substance can burn the esophagus. These types of products can also be inhaled into the lungs during vomiting'; ATP 4-02.83 4-27 also says emetics are contraindicated when consciousness is impaired. Reviewer flag for the owner, from outside the kit: current poison-control practice no longer advises inducing vomiting, and salt water given as an emetic can itself poison; no kit source says this. Fix: at minimum add the ATP contraindication and keep 'conscious only'; recommended: drop 'or by giving warm saltwater' and consider dropping the induce-vomiting sentence, owner to decide. (2) The ask 'is this berry safe to eat' is not answered, though ATP 4-50 has berry rules ('Avoid white and yellow berries for they are frequently poisonous. About one-half of all red berries are poisonous.'; it also says blue or black berries are 'generally safe' and aggregated berries 'always edible' - owner to decide on those generalizations) and TC 21-3 7-41 describes baneberry (white or red berries with a black dot). Fix: add the protective lines attributed, or drop the ask. ATP 4-50's 'Consider plants with shiny leaves as poisonous' is also missing from the avoid list. (3) Hidden conflict to record: TC 21-3 7-40 'Most plants that grow in cold regions can be eaten. The water hemlock and the baneberry are the only poisonous plants', contradicted by ATP's poisonous-plant list (death camas, poison and water hemlocks, etc.); do not adopt it, but list it in the conflict field. TC 21-3's water hemlock description ('one of the world's most poisonous plants', always in wet ground, hollow partitioned bulb, spindle-shaped roots, foul odor) is worth a warning line for Idaho.
